points.en: Deductive: the preacher states the points first, then tells stories as instances or proofs of each point.
Inductive: the preacher tells the story without giving away the point, and the hearer discovers it at the end.
Controlling story: one story dominates the whole sermon, running like a thread from first sentence to last.
Deductive puts the point before the story; inductive tells the story first and lets the point arrive or be discovered afterward.
Gives a situation for deductive, such as plain instruction or defending a truth that must be stated plainly.
Gives a situation for inductive, such as a truth that would be resisted if announced outright or that strikes deeper when discovered.
A point forced at the outset raises the hearer's defenses, while a story draws him in so he is not guarded.
Nathan told David a story, David condemned the rich man, and 'Thou art the man' then landed as a verdict David had pronounced on himself.
A truth the hearer discovers for himself, he owns.
One story dominates the entire sermon like a thread, and the preacher keeps returning to it, with other material woven around.
The chief danger is that the dominating story swallows the text, so it must stay anchored to Scripture and serve the Word.
Needs a true, well-earned story, since a weak one is felt for the whole sermon.
The goal is helping people make contact with God, so structure is a means and the outline was never the point.
Structure is not abolished: even the no-outline story sermon has a shape, and the three forms are disciplined structures serving the encounter.
Chooses one biblical truth and presents a deductive treatment: state the point first, then illustrate or prove it with stories.
Presents an inductive treatment of the same truth: tell a story that withholds the point so the hearer reaches it himself.
Keeps both treatments faithful to the text and clearly different.
In Unit 2 one overriding metaphor or image governs the message; in the controlling-story sermon one sustained story plays that governing role.
The controlling-story sermon is the narrative extension of the controlling metaphor: both organize the sermon around one picture, not a list of points.
Both must rise from and serve the text.
Strength: the story does its own work undiluted by over-explanation, and the hearer is trusted to feel and discover.
Risk: with too little interpretation the point may be missed, misread or left merely entertaining, so the preacher must make sure the truth lands.
The three-point outline is one legitimate form (the deductive), not the definition of preaching.
Inductive and controlling-story sermons are equally preaching when they carry the Word to the heart, as Nathan and Jesus show.
Cites Thielen: preaching is about contact with God, not points on an outline, while still valuing clear structure.
Names a text and chooses one of the three forms (deductive, inductive or controlling story).
Justifies the choice from what the text, the truth, the audience and the occasion require.
Sketches how the sermon would be shaped under that form, with the form serving the message.
